LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.BlockChannelCode: A length-n block channel code with M messages consists of an encoder from the message set to length-n input words and a decoder from length-n output words back to the message set.
The encoder of a block code is the function assigning each message its length-n input word.
The decoder of a block code is the function assigning a message estimate to each length-n output word.
Choose a uniform message among M ≥ 1 messages, encode it, and send its word through n independent uses of W. This gives the joint law of the message and received word.
Choose a uniform message among M ≥ 1 messages, encode it, and transmit through n independent uses of W. This gives the joint law of the message, transmitted word and received word.
For M ≥ 1 equiprobable messages, draw m uniformly, transmit its codeword through n memoryless uses of W, and decode the received word Y. The average error is Pr[decoder(Y) ≠ m] under this experiment.
With M ≥ 1, the probability of message m and received word y is (1/M) times the probability that the n-use memoryless channel produces y from the codeword for m.
For M ≥ 1, the message marginal of the joint message–output law is the uniform distribution on the M messages.
In the message–input–output law with M ≥ 1, the joint message–input marginal is the law of (m,encoder(m)) for a uniform message m.
In the message–input–output law with M ≥ 1, the input-word marginal is the pushforward of the uniform message law by the encoder.
In the message–input–output law with M ≥ 1, the input–output marginal is obtained by encoding a uniform message and passing the resulting word through the n-use memoryless channel.
For M ≥ 1, projecting the message–input–output law to its message and output coordinates gives the joint message–output law.
For M ≥ 1, the message marginal of the message–input–output law is uniform on the M messages.
For M ≥ 1, the output marginal of the message–input–output law is the law obtained by encoding a uniform message and sending it through the memoryless channel.
With M ≥ 1, the code error equals the decoding error computed on the message–input–output law using its message and output coordinates.
With M ≥ 1, the error probability is the probability under the joint triple law of the event that the decoder applied to the received word differs from the message.
The average error is (1/M)∑ₘ∑ᵧ Wⁿ(y|encoder(m)), where the inner sum runs over outputs y decoded to a message other than m and M ≥ 1.
The average error probability of a block code with at least one message is nonnegative.
The average error probability of a block code with at least one message is at most one.
A code with a single message has zero error for every channel and every blocklength.
A length-zero code with M ≥ 1 equiprobable messages has error probability 1 − 1/M.
For a length-one code with M ≥ 1, the joint law of its uniform message m and single received symbol is the channel joint law with conditional output distribution W(·|encoder(m)₀).
For a length-one code with M ≥ 1, the error probability is the average over messages m of the sum of W(b|encoder(m)₀) over symbols b whose one-symbol output word decodes incorrectly.
